explanations.answer: Confess their sins and their fathers' sins
explanations.explanation: Yes, friend. Verse 2 says they "…stood and confessed their sins and the iniquities of their fathers." They didn't only own up to their own sins, they owned up to their fathers' iniquities too. That takes some humility, and I know how hard that is when it's your own mess to admit.

explanations.answer: Bring offerings to the house of God
explanations.explanation: That's a fair guess, but this verse doesn't mention any offerings. What it says is that they stood up and "…confessed their sins and the iniquities of their fathers." The whole moment is about owning up.

explanations.answer: Choose new leaders for the whole city
explanations.explanation: Nope, nobody's running for office here. Verse 2 has them separating from the foreigners, then standing to confess "…their sins and the iniquities of their fathers." Picking leaders isn't part of this verse.

explanations.answer: To bless the LORD their God
explanations.explanation: That's it. The Levites say, "Stand up and bless the LORD your God from everlasting to everlasting…" It's a call to praise before they say anything else. I like that they start with who God is.

Close to the neighborhood, but no governor speaks in these verses. The Levites are the ones calling out, and they tell the people to "Stand up and bless the LORD your God…" The one being honored in this moment is God.

explanations.answer: To march out to the city gates
explanations.explanation: Marching to the city gates isn't in the verse, friend. The Levites say, "Stand up and bless the LORD your God from everlasting to everlasting…" The call is to bless the LORD. The people have plenty of time on their feet already.

explanations.answer: With God creating the heavens and the earth
explanations.explanation: Right, they go all the way back to the beginning. The Levites pray, "You created the heavens, the highest heavens with all their host, the earth and all that is on it, the seas and all that is in them." They didn't start with their own troubles. They started with who made everything.

explanations.answer: With Moses leading Israel out of Egypt
explanations.explanation: Moses does show up in this prayer, but not at the start. His name comes in verse 14, after creation, Abraham and Egypt. The prayer opens much earlier, with God who "…created the heavens, the highest heavens with all their host…" It's a long prayer, and it starts way back.

explanations.answer: With David bringing the ark to Jerusalem
explanations.explanation: David, Israel's king (2 Samuel 5:3), doesn't appear anywhere in this prayer. The Levites open in verse 6 with God who "…created the heavens, the highest heavens with all their host…" Their history starts at the very beginning.

Yes, Abraham. Verse 7 says God chose Abram, brought him out of Ur of the Chaldeans "…and gave him the name Abraham." The Levites remember that God picked him and named him. That's a big moment to bring up in a prayer.
The people in this passage are called Israelites, so I get why that one came to mind. But the name God gives Abram in verse 7 is Abraham. The text says God "…gave him the name Abraham."
Isaac isn't named anywhere in this prayer. The verse says God chose Abram, brought him out of Ur of the Chaldeans, and gave him the name Abraham. That's the new name the Levites remember.

True. Verse 8 says God made a covenant with Abraham "…to give it to his descendants." and then the Levites say, "You have kept Your promise, because You are righteous." They're standing there in hard times and still saying God keeps His word. That's the kind of memory worth holding onto.

It's actually true. In verse 8 God makes a covenant with Abraham to give the land to his descendants. Then the Levites say, "You have kept Your promise, because You are righteous." They say that about God out loud, even in a hard season.

explanations.answer: They acted with arrogance against Israel's fathers
explanations.explanation: That's what the verse says. The signs and wonders came "…for You knew they had acted with arrogance against our fathers." The Levites also say God made a name for Himself that endures to this day.

explanations.answer: They broke a treaty they made with Israel
explanations.explanation: This verse doesn't mention a treaty. The reason the Levites give is that God "…knew they had acted with arrogance against our fathers." When the text gives one reason, I'll take that one.

explanations.answer: They wanted Israel's land for themselves
explanations.explanation: The text never says that. In verse 10 the reason is that Pharaoh and his people "…had acted with arrogance against our fathers." Nothing about land grabs is in there.

Fire is right. Verse 12 says God led them "…with a pillar of cloud by day and a pillar of fire by night, to light for them the way in which they should travel." The cloud covered the day and the fire covered the night. I'd have been happy with a nightlight, friend.
Salt belongs in the dough, not in the sky. Verse 12 says the night guide was "…a pillar of fire…" lighting the way they should travel. That's what showed them the path in the dark.
Stone is a good, solid word, but it's not the one here. The passage says God led them "…with a pillar of cloud by day and a pillar of fire by night…" Fire is what lit up the dark for them.

True. Verse 14 says, "You revealed to them Your holy Sabbath and gave them commandments and statutes and laws through Your servant Moses." Moses was Israel's leader, and the Sabbath came to them along with the laws. The Levites remember it as something God revealed.

It's actually true. In verse 14 the Levites say, "You revealed to them Your holy Sabbath…" and that comes along with commandments, statutes and laws given through Moses, Israel's leader. The Sabbath is part of what God gave them.

Rock is right. Verse 15 says, "In their hunger You gave them bread from heaven; in their thirst You brought them water from the rock." Water out of a rock. I've squeezed a lot of things, but never that.
A river would be handy, but that's not what the verse says. The Levites pray, "in their thirst You brought them water from the rock." The water came out of a rock.
Clouds show up in this prayer, but they're busy guiding the people by day in verse 12. For the thirst, verse 15 says God "…brought them water from the rock." Rock is the answer.

That one isn't what the verse says. Verse 15 says God "…told them to go in and possess the land that You had sworn to give them." He told them to go in, not to stay out in the wilderness. The land was the promise.
False is right. Verse 15 says God "…told them to go in and possess the land that You had sworn to give them." Nobody was told to stay put. God sent them toward what He had promised.

explanations.answer: To take them back to slavery in Egypt
explanations.explanation: Yes, and it's a hard one to read. Verse 17 says they "…appointed a leader to return them to their bondage in Egypt." After everything God did to bring them out, they picked someone to lead them back. The very next line is that God did not forsake them.

explanations.answer: To lead them into the land God promised
explanations.explanation: That's what God told them to do in verse 15, but it's not what this leader is for. Verse 17 says they "…appointed a leader to return them to their bondage in Egypt." It's the opposite direction, and the prayer says it plainly.

explanations.answer: To build them a city of their own
explanations.explanation: No city-building here, friend. Verse 17 says the leader was appointed "…to return them to their bondage in Egypt." That is the heavy part of this passage, and the Levites say it out loud.

Anger is right. Verse 17 says, "But You are a forgiving God, gracious and compassionate, slow to anger and rich in loving devotion, and You did not forsake them." Read that one slowly, because it's the center of the whole prayer. It comes right after the people stiffened their necks and appointed a leader to return them to their bondage in Egypt.
That's a fair-sounding word, but the verse doesn't use it. It says God is "…slow to anger and rich in loving devotion…" Anger is the word that fits.
Slow to speech would be a very quiet God, and that's not what the verse says. The Levites call Him "…gracious and compassionate, slow to anger and rich in loving devotion…" Anger is the missing word.

True. Verse 19 says that even then, "…the pillar of cloud never turned away from guiding them on their path…" The calf was right there in verse 18, with terrible blasphemies, and still the cloud kept leading. The prayer says God did not forsake them in the wilderness.

It's actually true. After the calf and the terrible blasphemies, verse 19 says "…the pillar of cloud never turned away from guiding them on their path…" And at night the pillar of fire lit the way. God kept guiding them.

That's the one. Verse 21 says, "For forty years You sustained them in the wilderness, so that they lacked nothing. Their clothes did not wear out and their feet did not swell." Forty years of walking, and the clothes held up. I can't get a pair of socks to last a winter.
Mending is a nice idea, but the verse doesn't mention it. It says, "Their clothes did not wear out…" That was during the forty years God sustained them in the wilderness, so that they lacked nothing.

explanations.answer: They were traded for new ones
explanations.explanation: No trading happens in this verse. It says plainly, "Their clothes did not wear out and their feet did not swell." God sustained them for forty years, so that they lacked nothing.
Stars. Verse 23 says God "…multiplied their descendants like the stars of heaven…" Funny thing, I get a star in my sky for every finished cookie box. Theirs came from God multiplying them.
Clouds were busy guiding the people in this prayer, so I see why that one popped up. But verse 23 says God "…multiplied their descendants like the stars of heaven…" The comparison is stars.
Windows are a funny one, friend, but no. Verse 23 says God "…multiplied their descendants like the stars of heaven…" It's stars, the kind you'd see from my bakery at night.

That's not what happened. Verse 24 says, "You subdued before them the Canaanites dwelling in the land." Israel went in and possessed the land, and God delivered the kings and peoples into their hands.
False is right. Verse 24 says their descendants "…went in and possessed the land; You subdued before them the Canaanites dwelling in the land." The promise from verse 8 was coming true right there.

explanations.answer: Houses full of goods and wells already dug
explanations.explanation: Yes. Verse 25 says they took "…houses full of all goods, wells already dug, vineyards, olive groves, and fruit trees in abundance." Houses already stocked and wells already dug. That's moving into a kitchen where somebody already preheated the oven.

explanations.answer: Empty houses that needed to be rebuilt
explanations.explanation: The verse says the opposite. They took "…houses full of all goods…" not empty ones. Along with those came "…wells already dug, vineyards, olive groves, and fruit trees in abundance."

explanations.answer: Storehouses that were already picked clean
explanations.explanation: Picked clean isn't what the verse describes. Verse 25 says they took "…houses full of all goods, wells already dug, vineyards, olive groves, and fruit trees in abundance." It also says they ate and were filled, and delighted in God's great goodness.

Yes, and it's a heavy line. Verse 26 says, "They killed Your prophets, who had admonished them to return to You." The prophets had been urging them to come back. I think that one hurts to say out loud.
That's not what the verse says, and it's a heavy part of the prayer. Verse 26 says, "They killed Your prophets, who had admonished them to return to You." The prophets were there to warn them.
The text says nothing of the kind, and this is a hard verse. It says, "They killed Your prophets, who had admonished them to return to You." The Levites don't soften it.

That's not how verse 28 goes. It says, "But as soon as they had rest, they again did evil in Your sight." Rest came, and the trouble came right back with it. The prayer is honest about how quickly it happened.

False is right. Verse 28 says, "But as soon as they had rest, they again did evil in Your sight." Then when they cried out again, God "…heard from heaven, and You delivered them many times in Your compassion." The Levites don't hide the cycle, and they don't hide God's compassion either.

explanations.answer: He is a gracious and compassionate God
explanations.explanation: That's the reason the Levites give. Verse 31 says, "But in Your great compassion, You did not put an end to them; nor did You forsake them, for You are a gracious and compassionate God." The reason is who God is, not anything they did. I'm glad about that.

explanations.answer: Israel finally obeys every one of His laws
explanations.explanation: The verses right before this say the opposite. In verse 30, "…they would not listen…" Then verse 31 gives the reason God didn't put an end to them: "…for You are a gracious and compassionate God."

explanations.answer: The prophets beg Him to give them more time
explanations.explanation: The text doesn't say that. Verse 31 gives one reason: "…for You are a gracious and compassionate God." The prophets in this prayer were the ones warning the people.

They say the opposite. Verse 33 says, "You are just in all that has befallen us, because You have acted faithfully, while we have acted wickedly." The Levites put the blame on themselves, not on God. That's honest, and it's hard to say.

False is right. In verse 33 the Levites say, "You are just in all that has befallen us, because You have acted faithfully, while we have acted wickedly." They call God just and faithful, and they own their part.

explanations.answer: In the land God gave their fathers
explanations.explanation: That's what verse 36 says: "So here we are today as slaves in the land You gave our fathers to enjoy its fruit and goodness…" They say it twice, "…here we are as slaves!" Slaves in the very land that was promised to them.

explanations.answer: In the faraway land of Babylon
explanations.explanation: Babylon isn't mentioned in these verses. Verse 36 says they are slaves "…in the land You gave our fathers to enjoy its fruit and goodness…" That's what makes the line so painful.

explanations.answer: In the royal courts of Persia
explanations.explanation: The text doesn't put them there. Verse 36 says, "…here we are today as slaves in the land You gave our fathers…" The land is the one God gave their fathers.
Kings is right. Verse 37 says, "Its abundant harvest goes to the kings You have set over us because of our sins." The people go on to say, "We are in great distress."
Priests are in the prayer, but not here. Verse 32 lists them among those who suffered hardship. In verse 37 the harvest goes "…to the kings You have set over us because of our sins."
Prophets come up in this prayer, but not in this blank. Verse 37 says the harvest goes "…to the kings You have set over us because of our sins." Kings is the word that fits.

explanations.answer: Make a binding agreement in writing
explanations.explanation: That's it. Verse 38 says, "In view of all this, we make a binding agreement, putting it in writing and sealing it with the names of our leaders, Levites, and priests." After all that history, they put it in writing and sealed it. A prayer was spoken, and now the names go into the agreement.

explanations.answer: Rebuild the altar at the temple
explanations.explanation: That's not what verse 38 says. The people "…make a binding agreement, putting it in writing and sealing it with the names of our leaders, Levites, and priests." Nothing about an altar here.

explanations.answer: Send a message to the king
explanations.explanation: No messenger is sent in these verses. Verse 38 says they "…make a binding agreement, putting it in writing and sealing it with the names of our leaders, Levites, and priests." The writing is theirs, and the seal carries their names.
